messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Financial Analyst
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath, Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Hopelessness: I have no future, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mateo Reyes is a twenty-four-year-old Colombian-American man who works as a financial analyst at a mid-sized investment firm in downtown Chicago. He was referred for psychological assessment following a brief disclosure to his primary care physician, though he arrived at the intake appointment guarded and visibly reluctant, as though some part of him had not yet decided whether to stay.

Mateo served two years in the Army before his honorable discharge at twenty-two, including a seven-month deployment to a forward operating base in eastern Afghanistan. The event that appears to have fractured his sense of self occurred during a patrol in which his unit came under sustained ambush fire in an open, flat stretch of terrain — an exposed hillside with nowhere to take cover. In the chaos that followed, Mateo made a series of rapid decisions under fire that resulted in the death of a fellow soldier, a close friend he refers to only as "D." The precise sequence of what happened remains, by Mateo's own account, unclear to him — he cannot reconstruct it in order, cannot say with certainty what came first or what he chose versus what simply happened. What he does know, or believes he knows, is that he survived and D. did not, and that something he did or failed to do was the reason.

His memories of that afternoon are simultaneously vivid and incoherent. He can describe the color of the light, the sound of the rifle fire, the specific texture of the dirt, with a clarity that disturbs him — and yet the sequence collapses whenever he tries to hold it. Fragments arrive without warning: a muzzle flash, D.'s voice, the weight of his own body against the ground. These sudden intrusive pieces carry with them an immediacy that makes the past feel present, and it is this quality — the way the memory refuses to stay fixed in time — that has deepened his conviction that he is fundamentally changed. The confusion in the memory feeds directly into his appraisals of what happened: because he cannot reconstruct a coherent account, he fills the gaps with the worst available interpretation, which is that he failed, that he chose wrong, that the man who came back from that hillside is not someone worth knowing.

Those appraisals have become the architecture of his daily life. Mateo has come to believe, with a quiet certainty that he experiences as simple fact rather than distortion, that he has no future worth imagining — that whatever trajectory his life might have had was closed off on that hillside. He feels that he acted in ways that contradict everything he understood himself to be, and this sense of violated identity has left him feeling permanently outside the world other people inhabit. At the office, surrounded by colleagues discussing markets and weekend plans, he watches them as though through glass. He is present in body but describes himself as unreachable, a permanent outsider in his own life. These beliefs, in turn, have driven the strategies he has constructed to manage his days: he avoids any conversation about his deployment or his time in the Army, deflecting questions with practiced brevity; he avoids anything that might evoke grief — he has removed photographs, declined a memorial gathering for D.'s family, and stopped listening to music they shared. He also avoids open spaces wherever possible, taking interior routes through the city, choosing enclosed cafés over outdoor seating, something his colleagues have noticed and quietly stopped questioning.

The maintaining cycle has grown tighter over the past two years. The fragmented, vivid memories surface without warning and reinforce his belief that he is broken and culpable, and those beliefs make it intolerable to sit with the memories long enough to process them, so he turns away — from the grief, from conversation, from exposure — which ensures the memories remain unintegrated and the appraisals unchallenged. His social world has narrowed considerably; he has no close friendships in Chicago, and his family, who know only that he "had a hard deployment," sense a distance they cannot name.

What finally brought Mateo to seek help was a moment at work: standing at a floor-to-ceiling window on the thirty-eighth floor, looking out over an open expanse of lake and sky, he experienced a fragment so vivid he gripped the window frame to confirm he was still in the building. He told his doctor the following day. What he is most afraid of, he said quietly at intake, is that talking about it will confirm what he already suspects — that what happened cannot be explained in any way that leaves him as someone other than the man who let D. die.
